explanations.explanation: Peter, one of Jesus' twelve disciples, follows Him at a distance, all the way to the high priest's courtyard (Matthew 26:58). The rest of the disciples had already deserted Jesus and fled (Matthew 26:56), so Peter is doing something different here. I think he's trying to stay close and stay careful at the same time. Not easy to do, friend.

Gethsemane is the place where Jesus took His disciples to pray (Matthew 26:36), and I get why you'd picture Peter staying put there. The disciples did all flee (Matthew 26:56). But Matthew 26:58 says Peter followed Jesus right up to the courtyard. He went toward the trouble, not away from it.

Packing up for Galilee would be the sensible move, I'll give you that. But nothing in this passage says Peter leaves town. Matthew 26:58 says he followed Jesus at a distance, right up to the high priest's courtyard. He's walking toward the house, not away from it.
Peter goes in and sits down with the guards (Matthew 26:58). Sitting down next to them takes some nerve, friend. I'd have picked a seat by the exit, and then maybe a seat outside.

The scribes are in the house, gathered with the elders (Matthew 26:57). Peter is out in the courtyard, though, not in with the council. The text says he sat down with the guards (Matthew 26:58). Scribes were in the building, guards were in the yard.

I know the disciples would be the friendly faces here. But they had all deserted Jesus and fled (Matthew 26:56). Peter is sitting with the guards (Matthew 26:58). He's the only disciple we see in that courtyard, and that's a lonely seat.

The two witnesses say Jesus claimed, "I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days." (Matthew 26:61) Many false witnesses came forward before them, but the council did not find the false testimony it was seeking (Matthew 26:60). Then these two come forward and declare it. It's the temple of God they bring up, friend.

Rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem in three days would be quite a construction job. But that's not what the two witnesses say. They declare that Jesus said He was able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days (Matthew 26:61). Walls never come up.

That would make for an awkward moment, with the whole council sitting in Caiaphas' house while someone talks about knocking it down. Good thing that's not the claim. The two witnesses say Jesus said He's able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days (Matthew 26:61). The high priest's house isn't mentioned in that charge.

The high priest asks, "Have You no answer?" (Matthew 26:62), and Jesus remains silent (Matthew 26:63). The text doesn't tell us why, so I won't guess. What it does tell us is that He said nothing to those charges. Just quiet in the middle of all that noise.

Matthew 26:60 does say the false witnesses came forward and the council couldn't find testimony to use. But Jesus doesn't call anyone a liar in this scene. The text says He remained silent (Matthew 26:63). The high priest is waiting on an answer and doesn't get one right then.
The high priest asks, "Have You no answer?" (Matthew 26:62), and Jesus remains silent (Matthew 26:63). Nothing in the text has Him asking for His disciples. He just stays quiet.

The high priest says, "I charge You under oath by the living God: Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God." (Matthew 26:63) That's a direct question put to Jesus under oath. The charges about the temple don't get the final word here. This question does.

The disciples had fled (Matthew 26:56), and I could see someone wanting to know where they went. But that's not what the high priest asks. He puts Jesus under oath and says, "Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God." (Matthew 26:63) The question is about who Jesus is.

That's a fair question to ask somebody, but it's not this one. The high priest charges Jesus under oath by the living God and says, "Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God." (Matthew 26:63) He's not asking about travel plans. He's asking who Jesus is.

The high priest tears his clothes and declares, "He has blasphemed!" (Matthew 26:65) Jesus had just answered the question and told them they would see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power (Matthew 26:64). That's what comes right before the high priest says it. Blasphemy is the charge he makes.

Lying is a charge you'd expect when people are hunting for false testimony. But the high priest doesn't say Jesus lied. He tears his clothes and declares, "He has blasphemed!" (Matthew 26:65). That's the word he uses.
Boasting is a word you might reach for, friend. But the high priest uses a different one. He tears his clothes and declares, "He has blasphemed!" (Matthew 26:65).

explanations.answer: They have all heard it themselves
explanations.explanation: The high priest says, "Why do we need any more witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy." (Matthew 26:65) His point is that everyone in the room just heard Jesus' words with their own ears. Earlier the council had been seeking false testimony (Matthew 26:59). Now the high priest says they need no more witnesses.

explanations.answer: The witnesses have all gone home
explanations.explanation: Nobody in this scene is said to have gone home. The high priest says, "Why do we need any more witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy." (Matthew 26:65) The reason is what the council just heard, not who's still around.

explanations.answer: Jesus has asked them for mercy
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask for mercy anywhere in this passage. The high priest gives his own reason: "Why do we need any more witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy." (Matthew 26:65) It's about what the council just heard.

The high priest asks, "What do you think?" and the council answers, "He deserves to die…" (Matthew 26:66) Back in verse 59, the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking false testimony in order to put Him to death. I think this is a heavy moment, friend.

The text says the council did answer him. When the high priest asks, "What do you think?" they say, "He deserves to die…" (Matthew 26:66) That matches what the chief priests and the Sanhedrin wanted all along (Matthew 26:59). It's a heavy verse, and it happened just as written.

explanations.answer: He doesn't know what she's talking about
explanations.explanation: The servant girl says, "You also were with Jesus the Galilean…" and Peter denies it before them all: "I do not know what you are talking about." (Matthew 26:69-70) I think this is a rough moment for Peter, since he followed Jesus all the way to this courtyard (Matthew 26:58). It's the first of the denials.

explanations.answer: He's proud to follow Jesus of Galilee
explanations.explanation: I wish that one were the answer, friend. But the text says Peter denied it before them all: "I do not know what you are talking about." (Matthew 26:70). He doesn't speak up for Jesus here.

explanations.answer: He's just a traveler passing through
explanations.explanation: That line isn't in the text. Peter denies it before them all: "I do not know what you are talking about." (Matthew 26:70). He answers what she said directly, not with a travel story.

When Peter has gone out to the gateway, another servant girl sees him and tells the people there, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." (Matthew 26:71) Different girl, different spot. Peter changed locations, and the same claim followed him.

The text says it did happen. Peter goes out to the gateway, and another servant girl sees him and says to the people there, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." (Matthew 26:71) She's a second servant girl, not the first. Moving to a new spot didn't get Peter away from the claim.

Matthew 26:72 says Peter denied it again with an oath, saying, "I do not know the man!" That's the second denial, and it's stronger than the first one. In verse 70, he only said he didn't know what she meant. Now he's put an oath behind it.
Peter never calls the girl a liar, at least not in Matthew. What he does is deny it again with an oath: "I do not know the man!" (Matthew 26:72). The denial is just stronger than before.
That would be a creative dodge, friend, but it isn't in the text. Matthew 26:72 says Peter denied it again with an oath: "I do not know the man!" He doesn't bring up where he's from.

The people standing nearby say, "Surely you are one of them, for your accent gives you away." (Matthew 26:73) The first two times it was servant girls, and this time it's a group standing close. That's more people talking to one man.

No sword comes up in this part of the passage. The people standing nearby say, "Surely you are one of them, for your accent gives you away." (Matthew 26:73). It's something about how Peter sounded that gave him away.

A cloak is a good guess, since we do like our clues to be visible. But the text says the people standing nearby told Peter, "Surely you are one of them, for your accent gives you away." (Matthew 26:73). It's what they heard, not what he wore.

Matthew 26:74 says Peter began to curse and swear to them, and he says, "I do not know the man!" The first denial was words, the second an oath, and now this. And right then a rooster crowed. Peter is in deep, friend.

That's not what Matthew records. He says Peter began to curse and swear to them, and Peter says, "I do not know the man!" (Matthew 26:74). Nothing in the scene has him laughing. It's a heavy moment, friend.
Peter doesn't beg anybody to leave. Matthew says he began to curse and swear to them, and he says, "I do not know the man!" (Matthew 26:74). He's still pressing the denial.

Peter remembers the word Jesus had spoken: "Before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." (Matthew 26:75) Count them up with me: the servant girl, the second servant girl, and the people standing nearby. That makes three. Jesus' word held true down to the number.

Two denials is close, and the servant girls did account for two of them. But there was a third, when the people standing nearby came up to Peter (Matthew 26:73-74). Jesus said, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." (Matthew 26:75). The count is three.
Seven would be a lot of denials for Peter. The words Peter remembers are, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." (Matthew 26:75). Three is the number.

That's not what the text says, friend. Matthew 26:75 says Peter remembered the word Jesus had spoken, and then he "…went outside and wept bitterly." He doesn't head back in to find Jesus. He goes out, and he weeps.

The text says Peter remembered the word Jesus had spoken, and then he "…went outside and wept bitterly." (Matthew 26:75) He doesn't go back inside. He steps away from the courtyard and cries. I think that's a man whose heart just hit the floor.
